name: Abstract Factory
intent: Create whole families of related objects that are guaranteed to belong together, without naming their concrete classes.
scenario: A UI toolkit builds buttons and checkboxes. In the Light theme every widget must be Light, in the Dark theme every widget must be Dark, and the two must never be mixed.
problem: The form code creates a Button and a Checkbox. If it picks each widget's class separately, a Dark button can end up next to a Light checkbox. Every new theme means hunting down every place that creates widgets.
solution: Define a factory interface with one creation method per product (createButton, createCheckbox). Each theme implements it and returns only its own family. The client receives one factory and cannot accidentally mix families.
pain: Every widget needs its own if/else on the theme
Nothing prevents a Dark button next to a Light checkbox
A new theme means editing every creation site
The form knows every concrete widget class
benefits: The form receives one factory and asks it for widgets
A factory returns one consistent family, so mixing is impossible
A new theme is one new factory, no edits to the form
The form only knows the Button and Checkbox interfaces
whenToUse: Your code must work with several families of related products
Products from one family are designed to be used together
You want to swap the whole family in one place (theme, platform, database vendor)
whenNotToUse: There is only one family, or only one product type: Factory Method is lighter
Families rarely change and mixing is harmless
Adding a new product type is common: every factory then has to change
pitfalls: Adding a new product (a Slider) means editing the factory interface and every concrete factory
Many small classes: products times families
Often confused with Factory Method; Abstract Factory is a set of factory methods for related products
Needs a place to choose the concrete factory once, usually at startup
